paras: The lynching of Frank Bruce's accused killer was the killing by a mob, in Tensas Parish, Louisiana, in early 1881, of an unnamed Black man arrested for the murder of a store clerk. The man was seized from custody on the way to jail, and the case survives in a single five-line item in the Donaldsonville Chief of March 12, 1881.

Frank Bruce worked as a clerk in the store of a Mr. Lemley in Tensas Parish. According to the Donaldsonville Chief, Bruce had been "recently" killed by a "colored man," whom the paper called "the murderer" although he had not been tried.

The accused man was arrested for the killing. While he was being taken to jail, a mob seized him and lynched him. The item gives no name for him, no date, no town within the parish, no account of how he was killed and no size for the mob.
No report of an inquest, of arrests among the mob, or of any official response appears in the coverage.

The Donaldsonville Chief, published in Donaldsonville, Louisiana, printed the case without a headline among brief state and national notes, between a report of a levee break on Bayou Lafourche and news of Senate appointments. Its wording was flat and brief, treating the clerk's killing as established fact and reporting the lynching in a single clause without comment. No other report of the case, in Louisiana or elsewhere, appears in the surviving coverage.

Only one report (A1, a short state-news item in the Donaldsonville Chief) was found; no second account, local paper, or inquest appears.

accounts.gist: Frank Bruce, a clerk in Lemley's store in Tensas parish, was recently killed by a 'colored man', who was arrested and then seized by a mob on the way to jail and lynched.

framing.detail: The Donaldsonville Chief ran the case as an unheaded state item between a crevasse report and national political news, calling the accused 'the murderer' and stating the lynching without comment.
